title: Payment stocks: how to analyze card networks
description: Payment stocks: network effects, take rates and balance-sheet mirrors — how to read the card duopoly's economics with the universe's own numbers.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
# Payment stocks: how to analyze card networks

**Payment stocks are shares in companies routing the message between card and merchant account — lending no money themselves: the credit risk sits with the issuing bank, the network takes its fee for moving the transaction through the system.** [The course on network effects](/kurser/v15-natverkseffekter) calls the card duopoly the market's purest two-sided network; AK1A's universe carries two listed carriers — Visa at 689 billion dollars in market value, Mastercard at 497 — the finance branch's unfilled subfamily beside banks, insurers and investment companies. Here is the analysis, with the course's and universe's numbers.

## The revenue engine — volume, value and the take rate

Revenue multiplies three factors: transactions, average value, and the share the network keeps — the take rate. The course's example: a payment volume of 1,000 billion dollars at a fee of 0.25 percent gives 1,000 × 0.0025 = 2.5 billion dollars in revenue; the volume grows on three wheels — more cards, higher purchases, more consumption by card. Visa's revenue grew from 29.3 to 40.0 billion dollars between fiscal 2022 and 2025 — plus 36.5 percent, 10.9 percent per year — Mastercard from 22.2 to 32.8 billion: plus 47.5 percent, 13.8 percent per year. Earnings followed: Visa 14.6 to 19.9 billion dollars, Mastercard 9.9 to 15.0 — the same model, different maturity. Rule one: decompose growth into volume and take rate — transactions follow consumption, fees have a ceiling.

## Network effects — the duopoly's moat

The card network is a two-sided market: cardholders want merchants accepting their card, merchants want networks the payers carry in their wallets. Every new user raises the value for all already in — the mechanics [the network effects analysis](/blogg/v15-natverkseffekter-analys) owns, carrying the duopoly through four decades of shifts. The moat deepens through [switching costs](/kurser/mt-05-byteskostnader-och-inlasning): changing networks means millions of merchants replacing equipment, agreements, routines — nobody moves first without losing volume. The universe's note: payment networks without lending risk — debts sit with issuing banks, the network carries the routing. The contrast to [the banking sector](/kurser/se-24-banksektorn), where credit losses drive boom and bust: here the balance sheet is thin, the income statement administrative. New technologies face one question — can they gather both sides at once? So far they sit on top of the networks.

## The world of margins — when gross margin is almost 100 percent

The cost structure differs from the cycle industries: Visa's gross margin stands at 97.7 percent, Mastercard's at 100.0 — revenue and gross profit are the same number; no cost of goods exists. The cost layer is operations, staff, marketing — compare [the margin ladder's](/kurser/ln-03-marginaltrappan-och-operativ-havstavng) plants and furnaces, where margin defines the business. The capital need is lean: Mastercard's capex runs at 0.4 to 0.5 billion dollars per year — less than marketing — and cash flow scales nearly one to one with revenue: Visa's free cash flow grew from 17.9 to 21.6 billion dollars over the period, Mastercard's from 10.8 to 17.2 — plus 17.0 percent per year. [Cash flow analysis's](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen) cleanest exhibit: growth without reinvested capital. Net conversion lands at 46 to 51 percent of revenue — between operating income and the post-tax level, worlds from manufacturers' digits. [The gross margin analysis](/blogg/v07-bruttomarginal-analys) maps the ladder's geography: the payment network at one end, the mine and steel mill at the other.

## The balance sheet's mirror art — ROE, buybacks and the P/B trap

Here is the industry's biggest trap. Mastercard's return on equity (ROE) is reported at 241.2 percent, P/B at 89.6 — Visa's counterparts 61.2 and 19.9. The difference is an artifact of the buybacks, which take home book equity year after year: Mastercard's substance per share is 6.40 dollars against a price of 567.75 — nearly 89 times book value. The measure that answers is [return on invested capital](/kurser/roic-01-avkastning-pa-investerat-kapital): Visa 54.8 percent, Mastercard 93.8, against a cost of capital around 8 — the spread is the duopoly margin. The debt ratios need double vision: Mastercard's debt per equity is 4.40 against Visa's 0.68, and [the debt ratio's pitfalls](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig) apply — but coverage stands at 28.08 and 38.34, Mastercard's 24.6 billion of debt against cash of 11.6. Read [the ROE analysis](/blogg/v09-roe-analys) and [the P/B course](/kurser/v05-pb) together: book equity says almost nothing here — the substance is the network, not the balance sheet; [the solvency measure](/kurser/st-01-soliditet-och-rantetackning) reads against the cash flow's strength.

## The owner-flow ladder — dividends versus buybacks

The duopoly returns capital in two tracks of different weight. Visa's dividend is 2.68 dollars per share — 0.71 percent yield on a 22.8 percent payout — Mastercard's 3.48 at 0.61 and 19.1. The coupon is a by-product: Mastercard's repurchases grew from 8.9 to 12.0 billion dollars per year — around 80 percent of the owner flow — and it shows in the EPS series: earnings per share rose from 10.22 to 16.52 dollars, plus 17.4 percent per year against revenue's 13.8; the 3.6-point difference is the shrinking share count, not the operation. [The dividend guide](/blogg/utdelningar-101) owns the ladder; the rule: separate the tracks — the coupon small and slow-growing, the buyback large and cyclical — the latter mechanically inflates EPS growth. Recalculate at revenue level first, share level second.

## The risks — regulation, litigation and cash's resistance

The main risks live in the rulebook and the courts. [Regulatory risk](/kurser/rk-06-regulatorisk-risk) owns the map: the EU's Interchange Fee Regulation (2015/751) caps the fees banks charge merchants for consumer cards in the EEA — 0.2 percent for debit, 0.3 for credit — and every further cap squeezes the take rate; [the regulation text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/SV/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32015R0751) is the primary source. In Sweden, supervision sits with [Finansinspektionen](https://www.finansinspektionen.se/), which examines payment providers in the PSD2 track — the field carries a paradox: cash usage among the world's lowest, [the Riksbank](https://www.riksbank.se/) follows it in its payments reports, Swish has made direct payment a habit — yet e-commerce and travel still run through the cards: Swish is locked to Sweden and the krona, the card crosses borders. Litigation is the third risk; Visa's fiscal 2025 carries the evidence: net income grew only 2.0 percent while operating income rose 11.7 — the 9.7-percentage-point gap carries provisions for ongoing disputes. Read the notes before the multiple: provisions swing results without the operation doing so.

## Valuing payment stocks — a priced duopoly margin

Valuation shows a market treating the duopoly as one system: Visa trades at P/E 31.98, Mastercard at 31.53 — nearly identical multiples — with EV/EBIT at 23.5 and 24.3. The free-cash-flow yield stands at 3.0 and 3.4 percent. But [the P/E's warnings](/kurser/km-009-pe) apply as always: the PEG ratios are 1.38 for Visa, 1.86 for Mastercard — both above one: the growth is priced, not free; Visa's forward P/E of 25.98 against a trailing 31.98 implies an expectation of plus 23.1 percent. By [sector analysis's method](/kurser/se-16-sektoranalysens-metod): which growth must justify the multiple, against which [sector median](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2) it is read. A moat too wide to dig anew is not a multiple too wide to pay for: the first is a fact, the second a price.

## Checklist: seven questions when you analyze payment stocks

1. **The volume engine** — how much of the growth is transactions and values, how much is take rate? The former follows consumption, the latter has a regulatory ceiling.
2. **The network's two sides** — what is the switching cost for merchants, cardholders and banks? Whose moat is widest?
3. **The nature of the margin** — gross margin near 100 percent: what do operations and marketing cost per revenue dollar? Does cash flow scale with revenue (capex below marketing is the signature)?
4. **The balance sheet's glass** — ROE above 100 percent and P/B in the tens are buyback artifacts: read ROIC against the cost of capital, coverage and cash instead.
5. **The owner-flow tracks** — how large a share of payouts goes through repurchases? Compare EPS growth with revenue growth: the difference is the share count, not the operation.
6. **The regulation and litigation map** — where do the interchange caps, the supervision and the provisions live? The operating-versus-net gap reveals the position.
7. **The multiple against the margin** — PEG above one: what fill does the price require? Normalize for dispute years first.

Payment stocks reward the reader who separates routing from lending — then reads the balance sheet as a mirror of the buybacks, not the operation's capital. The whole is in [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026); the volume and take-rate examples are the course's constructions.

_Sources: AK1A's universe (Yahoo Finance and MarketStack, raw data September 2026); [Visa](https://www.visa.com/); [Mastercard investor relations](https://investor.mastercard.com/); [the Interchange Fee Regulation (EU) 2015/751](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/SV/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32015R0751); [Finansinspektionen](https://www.finansinspektionen.se/); [the Riksbank](https://www.riksbank.se/). mastercard.com does not answer automated checks and is mentioned without a link. Worked examples from the Network Effects course._

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
